title: Rice Blast
text: Rice blast is a fungal disease of rice caused by Magnaporthe grisea (Pyricularia grisea). The disease can affect rice at any growth stage and may affect leaves, nodes, panicles, and seeds. Depending on the infected plant part, it is referred to as leaf blast, node blast, panicle blast, or neck blast. The common symptom is spindle-shaped leaf spots with brown or reddish/yellowish-brown margins, ashy centers, and pointed ends. Fully developed lesions are normally 1.0–1.5 cm long and 0.3–0.5 cm wide. Infected nodes may become black and rot. Infection at the base of the panicle can cause rotten neck or neck rot, resulting in the panicle falling off. Severe infection may affect secondary branches and grains, causing partly filled grains known as whiteheads. Disease development is favoured by low night temperatures of 17–20°C, high humidity, foggy and dark weather conditions, excessive nitrogen fertilizer application, and high plant density. Susceptible rice varieties listed by the Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture include Bg 358, Bg 357, Bg 360, Bw 367, At 373, and Bg 94/1. Management during the crop season includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart and practising weed management. For the following season after infection, management includes using resistant varieties such as Bg 403, Bg 406, Bg 366, Bg 359, Bw 361, and Bg 250; using certified disease-free seed paddy; adding burnt paddy husk at 250 kg per acre to the soil during land preparation; and avoiding the addition of disease-infected straw.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Rice Blast

title: Sheath Blight
text: Sheath blight is a fungal disease of rice caused by Thanatephorus cucumeris (Rhizoctonia solani). Symptoms usually appear at the base of the stem near the water level and may spread to leaves and panicles. Rice is particularly vulnerable during the maximum tillering and flowering stages. Initial lesions develop on the leaf sheath near the water or soil surface and may be oval or ellipsoidal before becoming larger and irregular. Lesions may have white centers with green, brown, and orange coloration. When the flag leaf is infected, panicle exertion can be affected. The fungus forms sclerotia on the leaf sheath surface, which can survive in soil for years. Disease development is favoured by high temperatures up to 40°C, high humidity above 90%, excessive nitrogen fertilizer, foggy and dark conditions, shade, high plant density, and varieties with many tillers. Almost all rice varieties in Sri Lanka are susceptible. Management includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart and practising weed management. If the disease spreads rapidly, the Department of Agriculture recommends specific fungicides. For the following season, recommended practices include using certified disease-free seed paddy, deep ploughing to bury infected plant residues, using the recommended seed rate, maintaining an average plant population, adding burnt paddy husk during land preparation, and avoiding infected straw. There are no genetically resistant rice varieties to this disease, although varieties with a clean plant base may escape the disease.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Sheath Blight

title: Brown Spot
text: Brown spot is a fungal disease of rice caused by Cochliobolus miyabeanus (Bipolaris oryzae). It is a seed-borne disease that can affect coleoptiles, leaves, leaf sheaths, immature florets, panicle branches, glumes, and grains. The disease may be present from plant emergence but becomes more prevalent as plants approach maturity and leaves begin to senesce. Symptoms include brown circular to oval spots on coleoptiles, which can cause seedling blight and result in sparse stands and weak plants. Leaf spots range from small dark brown or reddish-brown spots to larger oval or circular spots with dark brown margins and light reddish-brown or grey centers. Similar spots may occur on leaf sheaths and hulls. Infection of glumes can cause black discoloration, while infection of immature florets can hinder grain development and result in lightweight or chalky kernels. Economic losses are more significant when the fungus attacks panicles and grains. Disease development is favoured by temperatures of 16–36°C, high humidity of 86–100%, soils with low nutrient levels or problem soils such as saline or iron-toxic soils, and drought. Management includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart and practising weed management. For the following season, recommended practices include improving soil quality with organic fertilizer, using certified disease-free seed paddy, adding burnt paddy husk at 250 kg per acre during land preparation, avoiding infected straw, treating seed paddy with hot water at 53–54°C for 10–12 minutes, treating seeds with a seed-protectant fungicide, crop rotation, and proper land levelling.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Brown Spot

title: False Smut
text: False smut is a fungal disease of rice caused by Ustilaginoidea virens. It mainly affects mature panicles and grains, with symptoms becoming visible as grains mature. When a grain becomes fully developed, the pericarp may split slightly, allowing the pathogen to enter and develop inside the grain. The seed coat remains green while orange to brown-green fungal structures develop within the grain. The disease may occur in one or more grains of a mature panicle. Later, the outer covering ruptures and exposes greenish-black spores, and the affected grain may be replaced by one or more sclerotia. Disease development is favoured by temperatures of 25–35°C, high humidity, rain and wind during flowering, excessive nitrogen fertilizer, high plant density, and weeds. Susceptible varieties listed by the Department of Agriculture include Bw 367 and Bg 403. Management during the crop season includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart and practising water management. For the following season, recommended practices include using certified disease-free seed paddy, weed management, adding burnt paddy husk during land preparation, avoiding infected material, and maintaining appropriate water and plant population management.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - False Smut

title: Leaf Scald
text: Leaf scald is a fungal disease of rice caused by Monographella albescens (Microdochium oryzae). It is common and can sometimes be severe in major rice-growing districts in Sri Lanka. The disease affects mature leaves, panicles, and seedlings and is seed-borne, surviving between seasons through infected seeds. Lesions usually begin at the tips or edges of leaf blades and develop a chevron pattern of light tan and darker reddish-brown areas. The leading edge of lesions may appear yellow to gold, causing affected rice fields to have a yellow or golden appearance. Lesions from leaf edges may have an indistinct mottled pattern, and affected leaves eventually dry and become straw-coloured. When panicles are infected, developing florets or grain hulls may show uniform light to dark reddish-brown discoloration, and the disease can cause sterility or abortion of developing kernels. Management during the crop season includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart. For the following season, recommended practices include using certified disease-free seed paddy, weed management, adding burnt paddy husk at 250 kg per acre during land preparation, and avoiding infected material.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Leaf Scald

title: Sheath Rot
text: Sheath rot is a fungal disease of rice caused by Sarocladium oryzae. It affects most prevailing rice varieties and is usually a minor disease affecting scattered tillers, although larger areas may occasionally experience significant damage. The disease mainly affects the uppermost leaf sheaths enclosing the young panicle during the boot stage. Symptoms include oblong or irregular oval lesions with grey or light-brown centers and diffuse dark reddish-brown margins, producing an irregular target-like pattern. Affected flag-leaf sheaths commonly develop reddish-brown discoloration. Early or severe infections can affect the panicle, causing partial emergence; the un-emerged portion may rot and the florets can become red-brown to dark brown. Grains from damaged panicles may become reddish-brown to dark brown and may fail to fill. A powdery white growth consisting of fungal spores and hyphae may appear on the inner surface of affected sheaths. Disease development during flowering to fruiting is favoured by temperatures of 20–28°C, high humidity, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer. Management includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart. For the following season, recommended practices include applying organic fertilizer to improve soil conditions, using certified disease-free seed paddy, weed management, adding burnt paddy husk during land preparation, avoiding infected straw, and managing insect populations such as sheath mites.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Sheath Rot

title: Narrow Brown Leaf Spot
text: Narrow brown leaf spot is a fungal disease of rice caused by Sphaerulina oryzina (Cercospora janseana). It affects leaf blades, leaf sheaths, pedicels, and glumes. Disease severity varies from year to year and generally increases as rice plants approach maturity. The severity also depends on varietal susceptibility and can result in severe leaf necrosis, premature ripening, yield reduction, and lodging. Typical lesions on leaves and upper leaf sheaths are light to dark brown, narrow and linear, and develop parallel to the leaf veins. They are usually 2–10 mm long and 1–1.5 mm wide. In highly susceptible varieties, lesions may enlarge and merge to form brown linear necrotic areas. Lesions on glumes are generally shorter but may be wider, while brown lesions may also occur on pedicels. Leaf sheaths may develop a netlike pattern of brown and light brown to yellow areas known as net blotch. Management during the crop season includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart. For the following season, recommended practices include applying organic fertilizer to improve soil quality, using certified disease-free seed paddy, weed management, adding burnt paddy husk at 250 kg per acre during land preparation, and avoiding infected straw.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Narrow Brown Leaf Spot

title: Bacterial Leaf Blight
text: Bacterial leaf blight is a bacterial disease of rice caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. It can affect rice during the seedling and maturity stages, mainly affecting the leaves. At the seedling stage, symptoms include wilting and yellowing of leaves or complete wilting of seedlings, known as kresek. Kresek may sometimes be confused with early rice stem borer damage. Kresek can be distinguished by yellowish bacterial ooze appearing from cut leaf ends when the leaves are squeezed, while affected plants are not easily pulled from the soil compared with plants damaged by stem borers. On mature plants, lesions commonly develop as water-soaked orange stripes on leaf blades or leaf tips. The lesions have wavy margins and progress towards the leaf base. The disease can occur in both irrigated and rainfed lowland areas and is favoured by temperatures of 25–34°C, strong winds, continuous heavy rain, high humidity, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer application. Management includes applying urea at recommended dosages or according to the leaf colour chart and ensuring good field drainage. When the disease is observed, water supply should be stopped and the field allowed to dry where possible. If complete water removal is not possible, water should be directed out through drainage ditches or watercourses. Drainage water from infected fields should not be diverted through disease-free fields where possible. Application of potassium fertilizer after disease detection can help manage further spread.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture - Bacterial Leaf Blight

title: Bakanae
text: Bakanae is a rice disease caused by Fusarium fujikuroi. The pathogen is primarily seed-borne, and infected or infested seed is an important source of inoculum. A characteristic symptom is abnormal elongation of seedlings after germination. Infected seedlings become unusually tall, thin, and yellowish-green and may become weak or die before transplanting. In mature plants, infected tillers may have pale-green flag leaves, produce adventitious roots at lower stem nodes, and develop leaves that dry from the lower part of the plant. Severely affected plants may die before maturity, while plants that reach maturity may produce few tillers and sterile or infected grains. Infected grains may show reddish discoloration. The disease can also persist through soil-borne inoculum and infected crop residues, while weeds around fields may contribute to pathogen survival. Disease severity is associated with the amount of infected seed-borne inoculum. Management focuses mainly on seed health, including the use of high-quality seed from fields free of Bakanae and appropriate seed treatment. Proper disposal of infected rice residues and weeds can also help reduce disease incidence. Prevention through healthy seed and suitable seed treatment is particularly important because resistant cultivars are not a well-established primary control strategy for Bakanae.

title: Stem Rot
text: Stem rot is a rice disease caused by Nakataea oryzae, formerly known as Magnaporthe salvinii. The disease usually appears during the later stages of rice growth. Initial symptoms are irregular blackish lesions on the outer leaf sheath, commonly occurring above the waterline. The infection can progress into the inner leaf sheath and culm, causing the leaf sheath to partially or completely rot. Internodes may become blackish and collapse, and severely infected plants may lodge before harvest. Stem rot is generally considered a monocyclic disease, and disease severity is closely related to the amount of initial inoculum present in the field. Sclerotia and infected plant debris remaining in the field after harvest are important sources of primary inoculum. Sclerotia can persist in the upper soil layer for several years under suitable conditions. After field irrigation, sclerotia may float on the water surface and germinate when they come into contact with rice leaf sheaths, initiating infection. Therefore, the amount and survival of sclerotia in the field are important factors affecting disease incidence and severity. Some gramineous weeds in rice fields can also become infected and may contribute to pathogen survival.

title: Bacterial Leaf Streak
text: Bacterial leaf streak is a rice disease caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola. It is commonly associated with high temperature and humidity and can develop during rainy conditions. The disease may appear from the tillering stage to the panicle-initiation or booting stages. Initial symptoms are short, fine, translucent, water-soaked streaks between the larger veins of leaves. When viewed against light, young lesions appear translucent. The streaks enlarge lengthwise between the veins and may become light brown or yellowish-brown. Under humid conditions, small yellowish-amber bacterial ooze droplets may appear on the lesions. In susceptible plants, numerous lesions may merge, causing large portions of the leaf to become brown, bleached, or grayish-white. Severe infection can reduce photosynthetic leaf area and may reduce grain weight. Continuous rainfall after disease appearance can promote severe disease development, while disease development may slow when rainfall stops and newly emerging leaves remain healthy. Bacterial leaf streak can be confused with bacterial leaf blight and narrow brown leaf spot. Bacterial leaf streak generally produces thinner, translucent streaks between the veins and may produce small bead-like bacterial ooze on the leaf surface. The pathogen enters rice tissues mainly through stomata and natural injuries and multiplies within leaf tissues. Infected rice seed is an important source of primary inoculum and can contribute to long-distance dissemination and initial disease development.

title: Grassy Stunt
text: Grassy stunt is a viral disease of rice caused by Rice grassy stunt virus (RGSV). The disease is transmitted persistently by the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens), which is the main vector and an important factor in disease spread. Grassy stunt occurs mainly in South and Southeast Asia and has also been reported in Sri Lanka and other parts of Asia. Typical symptoms include severe plant stunting, excessive tillering, short and narrow leaves, and an erect, grass-like appearance. Leaves may become pale green or pale yellow and develop numerous rusty, chlorotic, or yellowish spots that can expand into irregular blotches or stripes. Infected plants usually produce few small panicles with unfilled or discolored grains. Disease severity depends on the growth stage at infection. Plants infected at early stages can show severe stunting and major yield reduction, while later infections may cause less height reduction but can still result in severe leaf and panicle damage. Some infected plants may survive until harvest, and symptoms can remain visible in ratoon rice after harvest. Different RGSV strains can vary in symptom severity and their effects on tillering. Field diagnosis is commonly based on characteristic symptoms, but symptoms alone may not always provide a conclusive diagnosis. Confirmation can be performed using transmission tests with brown planthoppers or laboratory detection methods such as ELISA.

title: Ragged Stunt
text: Ragged stunt is a viral disease of rice caused by Rice ragged stunt virus (RRSV). The disease is transmitted persistently by the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens), which is the main vector and an important factor in disease spread. Ragged stunt occurs mainly in South and Southeast Asia and has also been reported in Sri Lanka and other parts of Asia. Early symptoms include delayed development of new leaves, short and malformed leaves, twisting of leaf tips, and breaks, notches, or indentations along leaf edges. As the disease develops, plants become stunted and may develop swollen veins or gall-like swellings on leaf blades and sheaths. Infected plants may show delayed flowering, incomplete panicle exertion, poor panicle development, and unfilled or discolored grains. Nodal branches may also develop on infected tillers. Symptoms can become less obvious on newly emerging leaves as the plant grows, causing some field infections to be overlooked, but symptoms may become more noticeable again at the heading stage, particularly on flag leaves, which can become short, deformed, and ragged. Disease severity and symptom expression vary among rice cultivars and growth stages. Early infection can cause severe damage and yield loss. Ragged stunt symptoms can resemble other rice viral diseases, particularly diseases associated with deformed leaves and vein swelling, so field symptoms alone may not always provide a conclusive diagnosis.

title: Tomato Damping-off
text: Damping-off is a disease of tomato seedlings that causes seedling death due to root infection. The causal pathogens listed by the Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture are Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia spp., Sclerotium spp., and Colletotrichum spp. Disease management includes preparing nursery beds on suitable land, heat sterilization, and appropriate seed and soil treatments. Recommended seed treatments include Thiram 80 WP at 5 g/kg of seed or Homai at 4 g/kg of seed. Recommended soil treatments include Thiram 80 WP at 7 g/5 L/m² or Homai at 5 g/5 L/m².

title: Tomato Early Blight
text: Early blight of tomato is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. Symptoms include dark patches with concentric rings on leaves, fruits, and stems. Disease management involves using recommended fungicides at the initial stage of disease development according to Department of Agriculture recommendations. The source lists Mancozeb 80% WP at 20 g/10 L of water, Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP at 12.5 g/10 L of water, and Metiram 55% + Pyraclostrobin 5% WG at 8 ml/10 L of water.

title: Tomato Late Blight
text: Late blight of tomato is a disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. Symptoms first appear on lower, older leaves as water-soaked grey-green spots. The spots later darken and white fungal growth develops on the underside of affected leaves. Disease management involves using recommended fungicides at the initial stage of disease development according to Department of Agriculture recommendations. The source lists Mancozeb 80% WP at 20 g/10 L of water, Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP at 12.5 g/10 L of water, and Metiram 55% + Pyraclostrobin 5% WG at 8 ml/10 L of water.

title: Tomato Target Spot
text: Target spot of tomato is a fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Symptoms include circular, dark-brown necrotic lesions in a concentric pattern on leaves, often surrounded by a yellow halo. The lesions can spread to the leaflets, while severe infection causes leaves to turn yellow, collapse, and die. Spots can also occur on stems and fruits. The Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture states that suitable fungicides for this disease are under testing.

title: Tomato Powdery Mildew
text: Powdery mildew of tomato is a fungal disease caused by Oidium lycopersicum. Symptoms include light-green to bright-yellow lesions on the upper surface of leaves. White powdery patches develop on the lower leaf surface when the fungus produces spores. Severe infection can result in leaf defoliation. Disease management involves applying recommended fungicides at the initial stage of disease development. The source lists sulfur 80% WG at 50 g/10 L of water, chlorothalonil 500 g/L SC at 30 ml/10 L of water, and carbendazim 50% WP at 7 g/10 L of water.

title: Tomato Anthracnose
text: Anthracnose of tomato is a fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum coccodes. Symptoms include die-back from apical buds, flower dropping, and black, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruits. Fruit infection can result in fruit rot. Management includes treating seeds with recommended fungicides before sowing and applying recommended fungicides at the initial stage of disease development according to Department of Agriculture recommendations.

title: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot
text: Septoria leaf spot of tomato is a fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici. Symptoms begin as water-soaked areas on affected leaves that develop into circular lesions with brown to gray centers. Disease management involves using recommended fungicides according to Department of Agriculture recommendations. The source lists Daconil at 15–30 ml/10 L of water, Mancozeb at 20 ml/10 L, Topsin at 6 g/10 L, and Carbendazim at 7 g/10 L.

title: Tomato Collar Rot and Root Rot
text: Collar rot and root rot of tomato are caused by Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia spp., and Sclerotium spp. The pathogens attack the collar portion of the plant. Infection causes the lower leaves to dry, followed by drying of the entire plant. The affected plant develops a characteristic wilting symptom and may eventually die.

title: Tomato Bacterial Wilt
text: Bacterial wilt of tomato is a bacterial disease caused by Ralstonia solanacearum. The main symptom is permanent wilting of the plant even when adequate water is present in the soil. A useful diagnostic symptom is viscous bacterial ooze that exudes from the cut end of an affected stem when it is immersed in water. Management includes using wilt-resistant tomato varieties, practicing crop rotation with legumes and cereals, and maintaining good field sanitation.

title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a viral disease of tomato transmitted by whiteflies. Symptoms include upward curling of leaves, yellow or chlorotic leaf margins, smaller-than-normal leaves, plant stunting, and flower drop. When plants are infected early in their growth, they may produce no fruit. Infected plants may occur randomly throughout the field. Management focuses on prevention through disease-free seeds, weed-free fields, field sanitation, removal of old crop debris, elimination of weeds, and reduction of the vector population using insecticides.

title: Tomato Curly Top Virus
text: Curly Top Virus (CTV) is a viral disease of tomato transmitted by leafhoppers. Symptoms include inward rolling of leaflets along the midrib. The petiole and midrib frequently curve downward, causing the leaves to appear drooping without actual wilting. Affected leaves become thick, crisp, brittle, and dull green, with purple veins. Management focuses on prevention through disease-free seeds, weed-free fields, field sanitation, removal of old crop debris, elimination of weeds, and reduction of the vector population using insecticides.

title: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus
text: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) is a viral disease of tomato spread by thrips. Symptoms include bronzing, leaf curling, necrotic streaks and spots on leaves, and dark-brown streaks on leaf petioles, stems, and growing tips. Infected plants become small and stunted. Ripe fruits may develop pale-red or yellow areas on the skin. Severe infection can cause extensive necrosis and plant death. Management focuses on prevention through disease-free seeds, weed-free fields, field sanitation, removal of old crop debris, elimination of weeds, and reduction of the vector population using insecticides.

title: Tomato Cucumber Mosaic Virus
text: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) is a viral disease of tomato transmitted by aphids. Early symptoms include yellowing, bushy growth, and considerable plant stunting. As the disease develops, leaves may become filiform or develop narrow, shoestring-like leaf blades. Leaf mottling is also a characteristic symptom. Management focuses on using disease-free seeds, maintaining weed-free fields and good field sanitation, and reducing the vector population using insecticides.

title: Tomato Cultivation and Management
text: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicon) is an important vegetable crop in the Solanaceae family and can be cultivated in almost all agroclimatic zones in Sri Lanka except the up-country wet zone. Suitable conditions include a temperature of about 21–24°C, soil pH of 5.5–7.5, and an elevation of 1000–2000 m. Addition of organic matter supports better growth. The recommended seed requirement is 200–250 g/ha. Suitable periods for nursery establishment are mid-March or the end of August. Raised nursery beds of about 1 m × 3 m and 15–20 cm height are recommended. Well-decomposed farmyard manure and topsoil can be mixed at a 1:1 ratio, and nursery-bed sterilization can be carried out by burning clean paddy husk and straw layers. Seeds should be treated before sowing according to the recommended seed-treatment method. Seedlings should be transplanted 14–18 days after sowing when they have 3–5 true leaves. Seedlings should be hardened before transplanting and thoroughly watered 12–14 hours before transplanting. Recommended field spacing is 80 cm × 50 cm. Land should be well prepared, supplied with decomposed organic matter, and provided with drainage to prevent water retention. For districts other than Badulla, the chemical fertilizer recommendation is 65 kg/ha Urea, 325 kg/ha TSP, and 65 kg/ha MOP as basal fertilizer 1–2 days before planting; 65 kg/ha Urea at 3 weeks after planting; and 65 kg/ha Urea plus 65 kg/ha MOP at 6 weeks after planting. For Badulla District, TSP is recommended at 215 kg/ha. Excessive watering, particularly during dry periods, should be avoided because it can cause fruit cracking. Fields should be kept free of weeds, especially during the first 3–6 weeks after transplanting, and weeding should be done before fertilizer application. Tomatoes are harvested when fruits reach the green-yellow stage and should be sorted according to size and quality and stored in a well-aerated place. Typical yield is about 20–30 tonnes per hectare, depending on season, variety, and climate.
